summary: Describes Time Division Multiplexing over IP (TDMoIP), a structure-aware method of carrying TDM signals over pseudowires. Being structure-aware helps it cope better with network problems, and it allows tricks like concealing packet loss. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Old telephone circuits put each call in a numbered slot in a repeating frame. This memo describes how to carry those frames across an IP network while keeping the frame structure intact, so that a lost packet can be patched over instead of raising an alarm on the line.

subtitle: Carrying old-style telephone circuits over IP while keeping the frame and channel structure visible.

tldr.problem: Telephony traffic rides on synchronous circuits with a fixed structure of frames and timeslots, and the standard way to move those circuits over a packet network throws that structure away, so a single lost packet causes an alarm rather than a small glitch.
tldr.mechanism: TDMoIP is a structure-aware encapsulation. It keeps the frames and channels visible so that lost packets can be concealed at the channel level, and it offers three ways of preserving structure: locking each packet to whole structures, indicating where structures start, or reassembling the structure at the far end.
tldr.outcome: The document is an Informational specification of the encapsulation, covering UDP/IP, MPLS, L2TPv3 and Ethernet packet networks, with AAL1 for circuit emulation and AAL2 for loop emulation.

today: RFC 5087 is an Informational document published in December 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies the encapsulation only; the pseudowire setup extensions live in a separate document. It is the structure-aware counterpart to the structure-agnostic RFC 4553, and it shares the fault vocabulary and the jitter buffer approach with RFC 5086.

sections.title: TDM Structure and Structure-Aware Transport
sections.content:
Telephony traffic is conventionally carried over connection-oriented synchronous or plesiochronous links, loosely called TDM circuits. With the spread of packet-switched networks, carrying those services over packet networks became desirable, and it can be done with pseudowires as described in the PWE3 architecture. The emulation has to keep the service quality of native TDM: voice quality, latency, timing and signalling features must be similar to those of existing TDM networks.

Structure-Agnostic TDM over Packet, SAToP, treats the TDM input as an arbitrary bit stream and disregards any structure in it. TDMoIP, the subject of this document, is structure-aware instead. A structure-aware method keeps the integrity of the TDM structure, so the pseudowire can better withstand network degradation. Individual multiplexed channels become visible, which allows per-channel mechanisms for packet loss concealment and bandwidth conservation, and TDM signalling becomes accessible, so mechanisms can exploit or manipulate it.

The TDM structures are standardized blocks of constant length. The familiar T1 and E1 frames are 193 and 256 bits long, and concatenating consecutive frames builds higher level structures called superframes or multiframes. T3 and E3 frames are much larger, and the GSM Abis channel uses larger structures still. A structure holds the data plus structure overhead: the 193-bit T1 frame carries a single bit of overhead and 24 bytes of data, and the 32-byte E1 frame carries a byte of overhead and 31 data bytes. Structured circuits frequently carry multiplexed channels, with a single byte in the frame, a timeslot, allocated to each channel. A frame of a channelized T1 carries 24 byte-sized channels and an E1 frame has 31. Because frames are sent 8000 times per second, one byte-sized channel carries 64 kbps. Structures are delimited by an easily detectable periodic bit pattern, the Frame Alignment Signal, placed in the structure overhead, which may also carry error monitoring and defect indications.

The difference matters when a packet is lost. With SAToP, a lost packet causes an all-ones pattern to be played out, which the TDM end equipment reads as an Alarm Indication Signal and which immediately triggers a severely errored second event, so SAToP suits only extremely reliable and underutilized networks. Structure-aware transport can explicitly safeguard the structure and so conceal packet loss effectively. It does not have to carry the structure overhead across the network: the frame alignment signal may be stripped by the sending end and must be regenerated by the receiving end, although other overhead may be carried because it may contain more than the alignment signal.

There are three conceptually distinct ways of keeping the structure intact. Structure-locking requires each packet to begin at the start of a TDM structure and to hold a whole structure or a whole number of them. Structure-indication allows packets to hold arbitrary fragments of basic structures and uses pointers to say where each structure starts. Structure-reassembly applies only to channelized TDM, where the sending end extracts and buffers individual channels and the receiving end reassembles the original structure from what arrives. Structure-locking is described in RFC 5086; this document specifies the other two. Structure-indication is used when channels are allocated statically or when interworking with existing AAL1-based circuit emulation systems is needed, and structure-reassembly when dynamic allocation is wanted or when interworking with AAL2-based loop emulation systems is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The difference is what happens when a packet is lost. If the structure is thrown away, the receiver has to send an alarm down the line. If the structure is kept, the receiver can patch the gap and carry on. This memo describes three ways of keeping it.

sections.title: The Encapsulation and the Control Word
sections.content:
A TDMoIP packet has the packet network headers, the TDMoIP control word and an adapted payload. The packet network headers are those of UDP/IP, L2TPv3/IP, MPLS or layer 2 Ethernet, and carry everything needed to forward the packet. Despite its name the protocol may run over several kinds of packet network. An interworking function may support several pseudowires at once and must keep context for each; distinct pseudowires are told apart by their labels, carried in the packet network specific layers, and since TDM is inherently bidirectional, two pseudowires in opposite directions are associated, though their labels may differ.

An optional 12-byte RTP header may appear, to allow explicit transfer of timing information. This is a purely formal reuse of the header format; RTP mechanisms such as header extensions, padding, RTCP, header compression and SRTP do not apply. The RTP timestamp is the packet creation time in units of a clock common to both ends; when no common clock is available, or the ends have sufficiently accurate local clocks, the RTP header should be omitted. If RTP is used, the fixed header must follow the control word for all packet network types except UDP/IP, where it must precede it. The version must be 2, the padding, extension, CSRC count and marker fields must be zero, the payload type must be allocated from the dynamic range, the RTP sequence number must equal the one in the control word, and the clock frequency must be an integer multiple of 8 kHz.

The 32-bit control word appears in every TDMoIP packet. Its first 4 bits must be zero when the packet network is MPLS, so that a packet does not alias an IP packet when forwarding devices inspect it deeply; for other packet networks the nibble may be zero, and in earlier versions of TDMoIP it held a format identifier. The L flag is set when the interworking function has detected or been told of a physical layer fault affecting the data being forwarded; in the trail extended case it must be set on loss of signal, loss of frame synchronization or an alarm indication signal. When L is set the packet contents may not be meaningful and the payload may be suppressed to save bandwidth, and once the fault is rectified the flag must be cleared. The R flag is set when the function detects or is told that TDM data is not arriving from the remote network, indicating failure of the reverse direction, and on receipt of an R flag the function should generate a Remote Defect Indicator. The 2-bit M field supplements the L flag: with L clear, 00 means no local defect modification and the other values are reserved; with L set, 00 means a TDM defect that should trigger conditioning or alarm generation, 01 means idle TDM data that should trigger no alarm, 10 means corrupted but potentially recoverable data, and 11 is reserved. Two more bits are reserved and must be zero. The 6-bit length field carries the length of the TDMoIP packet when padding is used to meet a minimum transmission unit, and must be used when the total packet length is less than 64 bytes. The 16-bit sequence number provides the common pseudowire sequencing function and detects lost and misordered packets; its space is 16-bit unsigned and circular, its initial value should be random and unpredictable for security purposes, and it is incremented modulo 2^16 separately for each pseudowire.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet carries a 32-bit header with a bit for a fault at the near end, a bit for a fault at the far end, a length field and a sequence number so lost packets can be spotted. An optional RTP header can be added when the two ends need to share timing information.

sections.title: The Payload Types
sections.content:
TDMoIP transports real-time streams by extracting bytes from the stream and then adapting them, and it offers two adaptation algorithms, one for constant-rate and one for variable-rate real-time traffic. For unstructured TDM, structured but unchannelized TDM, or structured channelized TDM with all channels active all the time, a constant-rate adaptation is needed, and TDMoIP uses structure-indication to emulate the native TDM circuit; that adaptation is called circuit emulation. For channelized TDM where individual channels, called loops in telephony terms, are frequently inactive, bandwidth can be conserved by transporting only the active channels, which gives variable-rate real-time traffic, and TDMoIP uses structure-reassembly to emulate the individual loops; that adaptation is called loop emulation.

TDMoIP uses constant-rate AAL1 for circuit emulation and variable-rate AAL2 for loop emulation. AAL1 must be used for structured transport of unchannelized data and should be used for circuits with relatively constant usage, must be used when the receiving function has to keep high timing accuracy, and should be used when high reliability is required. AAL2 should be used for channelized TDM when bandwidth needs to be conserved, and may be used whenever voice-carrying channels are expected to be highly variable. A third mode is defined for efficient transport of HDLC-based common channel signalling carried in TDM channels. The AAL family was originally developed to adapt application data to the rigid format of ATM, but the mechanisms are general solutions to carrying constant or variable-rate real-time streams over a packet network, they are deployed throughout the public telephony system, and reusing them simplifies interworking with existing AAL1- and AAL2-based networks.

In AAL1 mode the payload consists of at least one and perhaps many 48-byte AAL1 protocol data units. The number per packet must be pre-configured and chosen so the packet stays within the maximum the packet network allows, for example 30 for UDP/IP over Ethernet; a single unit per packet gives the lowest latency but the highest overhead. All implementations must support between 1 and 8 units per packet for E1 and T1 circuits, and between 5 and 15 for E3 and T3 circuits. Structured AAL1 keeps frame synchronization by embedding a pointer to the start of the next frame in the unit header, and structured AAL1 with channel-associated signalling keeps frame and multiframe synchronization with a pointer to the next multiframe and carries the signalling bits in a substructure.

In AAL2 mode the payload consists of one or more variable-length AAL2 units, each with 3 bytes of overhead and between 1 and 64 bytes of payload. Because AAL2 is inherently variable rate, arbitrary native service processing may be performed before a channel is placed in the payload, including testing whether it is off-hook, voice activity detection, speech compression, and fax, modem or tone relay. More than one unit belonging to a single channel may appear in a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to fill the packets. The circuit mode always sends the same amount of data and suits a whole circuit. The loop mode sends only the channels that are in use, so an idle line costs no bandwidth at all.

sections.title: Defect Handling
sections.content:
Native TDM networks signal faults by carrying forward defect indications, the alarm indication signal, and reverse defect indications in the bit stream. Structure-agnostic transport carries those indications transparently, but where a structure-aware mechanism strips the structure overhead that carries them, the defect conditions have to be signalled explicitly. Defects are signalled by setting flags in the control word, which mimics native TDM behaviour of embedding indications in the stream, and the flags exist for urgent messages, those whose contents must not be significantly delayed relative to the data they affect.

The operation is easiest to understand along the downstream flow from one TDM end system through its TDM network, through the first interworking function, across the packet network, through the second interworking function and its TDM network to the other end system. The goal is not only to detect faults in the first TDM network, the packet network and the second TDM network, but to localize them so that alarms are raised only in the appropriate network.

In the trail terminated case, only user data is exchanged between the two TDM networks. The interworking function acts as a trail termination function, and defects detected in the first TDM network are not relayed to the second. In the trail extended case, a defect anywhere in the first TDM network before the ultimate link makes the next TDM node generate an alarm downstream, and a break in the ultimate link is detected by the interworking function itself; either way the function raises the local defect flag in the packets it sends, extending the trail to the second TDM network.

Forward defect indications are generated by all network elements, but reverse defect indications only by trail termination functions. In the trail terminated case the first interworking function is such a termination and may generate a Remote Defect Indicator towards its own end system when it detects an invalid TDM signal. In the trail extended case it is not a termination and must not generate one, but sets the L flag instead, which causes the alarm indication to reach the far end system, which may then generate a Remote Defect Indicator. When the L flag is set there are four ways to treat the payload: the default is to fill it with the appropriate amount of alarm indication data, usually all ones, either copied from the received TDM data or generated by the function itself; with structure-aware transport of channelized TDM the payload should be filled with trunk conditioning, a preconfigured out-of-service code in each channel, which must be used when channels taken from several pseudowires are combined into a single TDM circuit; the payload can be suppressed altogether; or, if the fault is minor or correctable, the data can be kept.
sections.plainLanguage: When something breaks, the flag in the packet header says so, and the far end decides whether to send an alarm down the line, to mark the channels as out of service, or to send nothing at all. Which of those happens depends on whether the two telephone networks are meant to see each other's faults.

sections.title: Jitter, Timing and Congestion
sections.content:
A jitter buffer must be provided to compensate for the delay variation in any packet network: a block of memory that data from the network is written into at its variable arrival rate and read out at a constant rate to the destination TDM equipment. It partly hides the fact that a packet network rather than a synchronous network was traversed, at the cost of extra latency. Customary practice is to keep the buffer about half full, which minimizes the chance of it overflowing or emptying, so the added delay equals half the buffer size. The buffer length should be configurable and may be dynamic, growing and shrinking with the packet delay variation.

A packet sequence integrity mechanism must be provided to handle the infrequent losses and misorderings. It must track the serial numbers of arriving packets and act on anomalies; when packets are lost it must output filler data to keep the TDM timing, packets arriving in the wrong order should be reordered, and the processing should ensure that a proper frame alignment signal is sent to the TDM network. Inserting arbitrary filler may keep the timing but lead to choppy, annoying or even unintelligible audio. An implementation may instead insert a preconfigured constant value chosen to minimize the perceptual effect, replay the previously received packet, or, when the resources are available, estimate the missing sample values so as to minimize the perceptual error.

TDM networks are inherently synchronous, and somewhere in the network there is at least one extremely accurate primary reference clock, with long-term accuracy of one part in 1E-11, which gives reference timing to secondary nodes that distribute it further. Packets arrive with a random delay component, the packet delay variation. Reading data out of the jitter buffer at a constant rate removes much of the high-frequency part of that randomness, but the source clock information is not disseminated through the packet network, so the destination clock only nominally equals the source clock, leaving low-frequency wander. Four methods are described: timing provided independently of the packet network, either to the TDM end systems or to the interworking functions; a common clock assumed available to both functions, with the relationship to the source clock encoded in the packet as RTP timestamps or as the synchronous residual timestamp bits in the AAL1 overhead; and adaptive clock recovery, where the timing must be deduced solely from packet arrival times. Adaptive recovery uses observable characteristics such as the precise arrival time of a packet or the fill level of the jitter buffer over time, and because of the delay variation it must use filtering, with frequency locked loops and phase locked loops being well suited. Whatever mechanism is used, the output must conform to the jitter and wander specifications for TDM traffic interfaces.

On congestion, the AAL1 mode is an inelastic constant bit rate flow and cannot respond in a TCP-friendly way, though its share of the bandwidth stays constant, while the AAL2 mode is variable rate and the bandwidth used can often be reduced. Whenever possible TDMoIP should be carried across traffic-engineered networks offering bandwidth reservation and admission control, or forwarding prioritization and boundary traffic conditioning, with IntServ Guaranteed Service and Diffserv Expedited Forwarding as examples; the packets should not use the code point reserved for the default behavior, so that boundary conditioning works. Over a best-effort network, packet loss should be monitored to detect congestion, and if bandwidth reduction is possible it should be enacted, otherwise the pseudowire should shut down in both directions for a period. The document does not define exact detection criteria or shutdown methods. TDMoIP itself offers no guarantee of timely delivery, so the lower layers must provide it: layer 2 priority through the VLAN priority field, MPLS priority through the EXP bits, and layer 3 priority through the type of service field, with the switches and routers along the path configured to respect those priorities.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving end holds the arriving data in a buffer and plays it out at exactly the right speed, which smooths out the jitter of the packet network. When packets are missing it fills the gap with something chosen to sound as little as possible. Recovering the clock is the hard part, and there are four ways to do it.

sections.title: Security and Applicability
sections.content:
TDMoIP neither enhances nor detracts from the security of the underlying packet network, and relies on it for encryption, integrity and authentication; the security provided may be less than that of a native TDM service. When the packet network is MPLS, pseudowire-specific security mechanisms may be required, while for IP-based packet networks IPsec may be used, and TDMoIP over L2TPv3 is subject to the security considerations of that protocol. TDMoIP shares the susceptibility of pseudowires generally to pseudowire-layer attacks, and implementations should use whatever mechanisms for confidentiality, integrity and authentication are developed for general pseudowires. Random initialization of the sequence numbers, in both the control word and the optional RTP header, makes known-plaintext attacks on encrypted pseudowires more difficult. Pseudowire labels should be selected in an unpredictable manner rather than sequentially, to deter session hijacking. When using L2TPv3, a cryptographically random cookie should be used to protect against off-path packet insertion attacks, and a 64-bit cookie is recommended to protect against brute-force blind insertion attacks.

The applicability statement is honest about the differences from a native circuit. The end-to-end delay of an emulated circuit may exceed that of a native one. With adaptive clock recovery, the timing performance depends on the characteristics of the packet network and may be inferior. If the structure overhead is not transported over the network, the non-alignment data in that overhead is lost. When packets are lost, the mechanisms keep frame synchronization, and when the loss is properly concealed the effect on telephony channels is perceptually minimized, but the bit error rate is still worse than on the native service. In AAL2 mode, data in inactive channels is not transported at all, so it differs from the native service. And because native TDM connections are point-to-point while packet networks are shared, the level of security of the emulated service may be lower.
sections.plainLanguage: The security is whatever the packet network gives you, and it may be less than on a real telephone line. The memo also lists what the emulation cannot match: the delay is longer, the timing is not as good, and the error rate after packet loss is worse than on a native circuit.

fields.name: RES
fields.desc: Must be zero for MPLS so the packet does not alias an IP packet.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Local failure: a physical layer fault affects the TDM data being forwarded.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Remote failure: no TDM data is arriving from the far end.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Defect modifier, adding detail to the meaning of the L flag.

fields.name: RES
fields.desc: Reserved and must be set to zero.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the TDMoIP packet when the total is under 64 bytes.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: 16-bit circular counter for detecting lost and misordered packets.

viz.caption: THREE WAYS OF PRESERVING THE TDM STRUCTURE

cells: Each packet starts at a structure boundary and holds whole structures
Packets may hold fragments; pointers say where each structure starts
Static channel allocation, or interworking with AAL1 circuit emulation
Channels are extracted at the sending end and the structure is rebuilt at the far end
Dynamic channel allocation, or interworking with AAL2 loop emulation
The whole circuit, always, whether or not the channels are in use
Only the channels that are active, conserving bandwidth
